findings.defect: "the Min vertex $c_{10}$ is switched four times, $c_{8}$ twice" is false: $c_8$ is switched once and the vertex switched twice is the Min vertex $c_{11}$ — contradicted by the proposition's own displayed switch sets.
findings.evidence: I rebuilt Q_16 from the printed rows (all 32 rows leak; checked) and recomputed val_sigma / val^tau as componentwise extrema over all 2^8 counter-strategies in exact rationals (q16.py). The veto run from the printed start reproduces the printed sequence exactly: (∅,{9,10,11,16}), ({3},{10,12,13}), ({5,6,7},{10,11}), ({2,8},{10}), ({4},∅), halting at L=U=w*. Switch counts: {2:1, 3:1, 4:1, 5:1, 6:1, 7:1, 8:1, 9:1, 10:4, 11:2, 12:1, 13:1, 16:1}. c_8 occurs in exactly one C_max ({2,8}); c_11 occurs in two C_min ({9,10,11,16} and {10,11}). The printed C_max list in the same proposition already shows 8 once. Everything else in prop:q16 checks: 288 vertices (I built the actual 288-vertex game via lem:dyadic-row with the targets in vertex-index order — 8 Max, 8 Min, 270 avg, stopping, and its profile values agree with the normal-form solve at all 16 controlled vertices, q16build.py); the strict variant takes 5 rounds switching every vertex at most once; exactly three of the four c_10 switches (rounds 0,1,2) are val_sigma-ties, the fourth (round 3) is strict.

findings.defect: "at an additive cost of $O(1)$ vertices per reversal" is asserted, never proved, contradicts the same sentence's "$O(K^2)$ vertices", and is false for the only construction the proposition cites (lem:dyadic-row).
findings.evidence: Built SD(K) exactly as printed (chain k_j, Max x_j, rows p,q realised by lem:dyadic-row's pruned complete tree of depth d=K+3): N = 18,23,31,39,49,59,71,83,97,111,127 for K=2..12, increments 5,8,8,10,10,12,12,14,14,16, i.e. Theta(K^2) total and Theta(K) per reversal (sd.py). Three other leaf orders give the same growth: 21,29,40,50,63 / 18,23,29,35,41 / 21,29,37,46,60 at K=2..6 (sdcount.py). A Theta(K) build does exist — the Knuth–Yao lower bound on internal nodes for the two rows is 11,17,23,29,41,53,77,101 at K=2,4,6,8,12,16,24,32, i.e. linear — but the manuscript neither exhibits nor proves it, and lem:dyadic-row does not deliver it. The proposition's own bound O(K^2) is what is proved; "O(1) per reversal" is the stated moral of rem:readout(ii) and is unsupported.

findings.defect: "In the notation of \Cref{thm:bsi-tracks} the two-player form has $A=B=K$, so the first bound there is tight up to one" is false for the two-player form; the tightness holds for the one-player SD(K).
findings.evidence: I built the two-player mirrored SD(K) described in that paragraph (h-chain, Min u_j, v'->(q,p), mass redistributed) and ran BSI from the mirrored start, both variants, K=2..6 (sd2.py). Result: R=A=B=K with the claimed sets C_max={x_{t+1},v}, C_min={u_{t+1},v'}, L(u_j)=0 for every profile, halting at L=U. But m=k=K+1, so the first bound R <= m+(m+1)B = (K+1)+(K+2)K evaluates to 11,19,29,41,55 against R = 2,3,4,5,6 — slack by a factor Theta(K). The bound IS tight up to one on the ONE-player SD(K): there B=0, m=K+1 and R=K, so R <= m+(m+1)·0 = m = R+1.

findings.defect: "the measurements of \Cref{rem:bsi-br} were an artefact of instances whose all-switches runs are short relative to $|\Vmax|$" has the property backwards.
findings.evidence: rem:bsi-br's instances are L_n and G#. Recomputed: on L_n all-switches takes exactly n rounds from b=0…0 with |Vmax|=n (ratio 1) for n=1..7 (misc.py); on G# the document itself records 7 rounds with |Vmax|=4 (ratio 7/4). Both are LONG relative to |Vmax|. It is RD(n) — the new family — whose all-switches run is short relative to |Vmax| (1 round, |Vmax|=n).

findings.defect: "with $N=9n$ vertices" is not reproducible from the definition, which specifies the Theta_j, b_j gadgets only as "$O(1)$ vertices each over two shared chains".
findings.evidence: Building the definition literally — H=avg(t_0,t_1) doubling as the first vertex of both chains, d_i of value 2^{-i} and e_i of value 1-2^{-i} for i<=2n-1, Theta_j = avg(e_{2j-1},t_0), b_j = avg(t_1,d_{2j-1}), plus a_j, v_j, u_j and the two sinks — gives N = 9n-2 for n=1..8 (7,16,25,34,43,52,61,70), with the gadget values exactly theta_j and B_j and the game acyclic and stopping (rd.py). Only N=Theta(n) is supported by the text as written.

findings.defect: the citation "(\Cref{lem:gadget}, $O(1)$ vertices each over two shared chains)" is wrong for one of the two chains: lem:gadget realises only the values 1-2^{-i}.
findings.evidence: lem:gadget (l.964) damps an edge u->w with leak beta=2^{-m}; with w=t_1 its chain gives values 1-2^{-i}, which yields theta_j = avg(e_{2j-1},t_0) but not B_j. B_j = 1/2+4^{-j} = avg(t_1, x) needs x = 2^{-(2j-1)}, i.e. the dual chain leaking to t_1, which is not an instance of lem:gadget, and no combination of two values 1-2^{-p},1-2^{-q} averages to B_j for j>=2 (that would need 2^{-p}+2^{-q} = 1-2^{-(2j-1)}, a sum of 2j-2 distinct powers). The lemma that does supply arbitrary dyadic values is lem:dyadic-row (l.980), which the manuscript already has and cites in prop:leapfrog.

findings.defect: "all-switches halts after one round from every Max strategy" is false at the optimal start; it should read "after at most one round".
findings.evidence: The proof's own computation gives S_sigma = {v_j : sigma(v_j)=a_j}, which is empty at sigma_n. Recomputed at n=6: S_{sigma_n} = [] (misc.py), so all-switches performs ZERO productive rounds from sigma_n. Over all 2^n Max starts the maximum is 1 for n=1..7 (rd2.py), so the intended "at most one" is correct.

findings.defect: the vertex counts "$20,31,41,56,66$ for $K=2,\dots,6$ as built here" cannot be recomputed from the printed parameters plus lem:dyadic-row.
findings.evidence: Four natural leaf orders for the p,q rows at d=K+3 give (18,23,31,39,49), (21,29,40,50,63), (18,23,29,35,41), (21,29,37,46,60) at K=2..6; d=K+2 and d=K+4 give further values (sdcount.py). None is (20,31,41,56,66). The printed counts are all achievable (they exceed the minimum), but the build is not determined by the text, so the row is an unverifiable number. All of prop:leapfrog's mathematical content does check out: eta, gamma_j, Delta, alpha_j, beta_j, a_p, a_q are nonnegative dyadic, every row leaks, the game is one-player, acyclic and stopping, L_t(p)-L_t(q) = (-1)^{t+1}eta for t<K and (-1)^K eta at t=K, and all-switches takes exactly K rounds switching {x_{t+1}, v} for K=2..12 (sd.py).

findings.defect: "as every $v_i$ of the ladder $L_n$ of \Cref{thm:ladder} has" fails at $i=n$, and the \Cref points at the theorem rather than at def:ladder, where $L_n$ is defined.
findings.evidence: def:ladder (l.6766) sets v_{n+1}:=t_0 and w_{n+1}:=t_1, so v_n -> (t_0,t_1): neither successor is a Max vertex and neither is an average vertex, so the hypothesis "successors p in Vmax and q in Vavg with the same successor pair" fails. Checked on L_5: the pattern holds for i=1,2,3,4 and fails for i=5 (misc.py). Fix: "every $v_i$, $1\le i\le n-1$, of the ladder $L_n$ of \Cref{def:ladder}". The lemma itself is correct: val^tau(p)>=val^tau(q) with equality iff val^tau(a)=val^tau(b) held in all 908 (game, tau) tests on random stopping games carrying the pattern, and the last clause (p->q improving iff p is strictly switchable) follows from val_sigma(q) = mean(val_sigma(a),val_sigma(b)) with sigma(p) in {a,b}.

findings.defect: "For $N_k$ use \Cref{lem:kblind}(ii)" under-cites: (ii) is the operator/fixed-point statement, the value statement is (iii), and neither supplies the Min-side identity $\val^{\tilde\tau}=\val^{\tau}$.
findings.evidence: lem:kblind(iii) gives val^H = widehat{val^G} and val^H_{tilde sigma} = widehat{val^G_sigma}; the Min-side identity needs the same argument the proof spells out for N' — that N_k commutes with duality (it subdivides every edge with average vertices, a condition invariant under exchanging players and sinks) followed by lem:duality. The proposition is true: I compared BSI runs on G and on N'(G), N_0(G), N_1(G) for 150 random two-player stopping games, both variants, 900 run pairs, and every run had the same length and the same (C_max, C_min) sequence (nf.py). The proof also invokes lem:duality without noting its "off the sinks" restriction; here the sinks agree because duality exchanges them, but the proof does not say so.

findings.defect: the "designated entry vertex" need not exist, and the stopping argument is stated in the wrong order (it proves "no gadget vertex lies in a trap" before the step it needs).
findings.evidence: If all 2^d leaves carry one target (e.g. ell=1, r_1=1) the deletion step in the proof removes the root and the gadget has zero fresh average vertices, so no entry vertex exists; 227 of 4000 random admissible rows hit this (dyad.py). For d>=1 the lemma is repaired by an entry avg(w_1,w_1); at d=0 the bound ell*d=0 forbids even that, so a hypothesis (e.g. that the row leaks, as in every application) is missing. For stopping: a surviving internal node whose subtree carries no sink leaf does not itself force a contradiction; one must first descend to a controlled vertex, then use that both of its successors are gadget entries with a t_0 leaf below. The conclusion is correct. Otherwise the lemma verifies: on 4000 random rows the realised probabilities were exact and the bound of ell*d internal nodes was never violated; the consequence |C|+2+O(|C|^2 d) is consistent with prop:oneplayer-runs' 2m(m+1)log_2 D, and gives exactly 288 for Q_16 (|C|=16, d=6, targets in vertex-index order).

findings.defect: the proof needs $\{\val=1\}$ and $\{\val=0\}$ EXACTLY, but def:simorder, which it cites, explicitly licenses sound under-approximations of $Z_0,Z_1$.
findings.evidence: def:simorder (l.10190) says "Everything below uses only $Z_0\subseteq\{w^*=0\}$ and $Z_1\subseteq\{w^*=1\}$, so any sound under-approximation may be substituted." thm:top needs the exact sets: the step "every old average value is at most $1-2^{-a}$ by lem:denominator-sharp" uses that no surviving vertex has value 1, and a surviving average vertex of value 1 would beat both boosted maxima and break the reduction. The fix is one clause ("the exact sets, computed as in def:simorder"). Separately (out of range, but it makes the citation cheaper, not dearer): def:simorder's assertion that $Z_1$ "is not a single sweep" is wrong — $Z_1$ is the complement of the least fixed point containing $t_0$ in which a Max vertex needs BOTH successors and Min/average vertices need SOME, the exact dual of the $Z_0$ sweep. On 200 random stopping games the two dual sweeps returned exactly $\{w^*=0\}$ and $\{w^*=1\}$, including the self-loop configuration def:simorder cites as the obstruction (top.py).

findings.defect: notational and citation hygiene: $\Phi$ is overloaded a third time, $C^{>}_{\max}$/$C^{<}_{\min}$ are used without definition, "productive round" is never defined, and the appeal to lem:switch in $\bar G$ silently uses that $\bar G$ is stopping.
findings.evidence: $\Phi$ is $\sum_u x(u)$ in lem:switch (l.3329), the lexicographic pair $(M,|Z|)$ in cor:bsi-levels (l.7903), and the count of $U$-greedy Max vertices here. $C^{>}_{\max},C^{<}_{\min}$ are the strict-variant sets (this is the only reading under which "$C^{<}_{\min}\subseteq C_{\min}$" holds). That $\bar G$ is stopping is proved in cor:bsi-correct but not recalled. The theorem itself reconstructs without a gap and I could not break it: on 6000 BSI runs (both variants, random two-player stopping games) $\Phi$ increased strictly at every one of the 1725 rounds with $C_{\min}=\emptyset$, $\Psi$ at every one of the 1671 rounds with $C_{\max}=\emptyset$, every run halted at $L=U$, and all four inequalities plus the block bounds held with no violation (tracks.py).

findings.defect: "a superpolynomial family cannot be built by making one player work while the other idles, the failure mode of the disjoint union of \Cref{rem:bsi-gap}" mischaracterises that failure mode.
findings.evidence: In the disjoint union of $G$ with $\bar G$ neither player idles: both tracks switch. The failure is that the tracks are decoupled — on each component the veto reads $w^*$ of that component, so each track is prop:bsi-oneplayer's rule and both are short. rem:bsi-gap itself says exactly this ("each running in its own component and neither seeing the other's values").

findings.defect: "so the guide $\val^{\tau}$ can be as adversarial as a superpolynomial family would need it to be" overstates a Theta(N) slowdown, and is contradicted three sentences later by "is no progress on any lower bound".
findings.evidence: RD(n) exhibits n rounds against all-switches' one; a superpolynomial family would need the guide to be adversarial for superpolynomially many rounds, which the family (bounded by |Vmax| rounds, the thm:short-path ceiling for a one-vertex-per-round rule) does not show. The remark's own next sentences say so.

findings.defect: verification tags say "by the route", i.e. the manuscript itself did not check; the underlying claims are however correct — I verified them independently, at larger sizes than either tag claims.
findings.evidence: thm:readout: all-switches halts in at most one round from EVERY one of the 2^n Max starts for n<=7 (the tag claims n<=3); R_BR takes exactly n rounds switching v_{t+1} alone at round t, in both variants, for n<=7, and over EVERY best-response choice for n<=5 (the tag claims n<=4) — the best response is in fact unique at every sigma_t, since L_t(v_j) != theta_j always; BSI takes exactly 2n rounds with the claimed alternation for n<=7, both variants; all the proof's intermediate identities (L_t(v_j)=B_j and L_t(u_j)=theta_j for j<=t, L_t(v_j)<theta_j for j>t, U_t(a_{t+1})=f(theta_t), U_t(a_j)>B_j for j>t+1) hold exactly at n=6 for all t (rd2.py, misc.py). f(theta_j)<theta_{j+1}<B_{j+1}<f(B_j) holds for j=1..29. prop:leapfrog's two-player form: verified here for K<=6 (the paragraph claims K<=4).

findings.defect: "(Reproduced here on $150$ random stopping games with interior values.)" does not say what was varied, as the round's rules require.
findings.evidence: Reproduced independently here on 200 instances, varying |Vmax| and |Vmin| over {0,...,3} and |Vavg| over {2,...,5}, each first reduced by the two exact sweeps so that all remaining values lie in (0,1), with p,q drawn among the remaining average vertices: 66 cases with val(p)>val(q), 70 with <, 64 with =; in every case the maximum over Vavg of the enlarged game was unique and was c^{(m)}_p exactly when val(p)>=val(q) (top.py). The proof's algebra also checks: val(c^{(m)}_p)=1-2^{-m}(1-val p), val(c^{(m)}_q)=1-2^{-m}(1-val q+2^{-r}), both exceed 1-2^{-(r+1)} since (1+2^{-r})/2<1, old values are at most 1-2^{-a}<1-2^{-(r+1)} because a<r+1, and 4^{-a}>2^{-r}=4^{-(a+1)} rules out both a tie and the gap 2^{-r}.

findings.defect: "against the three reversals of \Cref{prop:allswitch-overshoot}" — that proposition records four Max vertices switched three times each, i.e. two reversals each.
findings.evidence: prop:allswitch-overshoot (l.3488): "switching four Max vertices three times each and four more twice each". Harmless if "reversal" is used throughout to mean "switch", which is how prop:q16 uses it too ("three of the four reversals of c_10" for four switches), but the two usages should be made uniform.

verdict:
VERDICT. The mathematics of the range is sound; the defects are all in printed claims and numbers, three of them false as written. Nothing fatal. sound=false only because of the three major items.

WHAT VERIFIED (all in exact rational arithmetic, my own code, from the manuscript's statements):
- thm:bsi-tracks. The proof reconstructs step by step with no gap: Phi(sigma,U) = #{U-greedy Max vertices} is non-decreasing across a C_min-empty round and rises by >=1 (strict variant: every switched vertex is strictly U-preferred; veto variant: lem:bsi-pairloc read in the strict variant gives Z ∩ C^>_max ≠ ∅ since C^<_min ⊆ C_min = ∅), so a maximal block has <= m rounds, there are <= B+1 blocks, R <= m(B+1)+B = m+(m+1)B; dually R <= k+(k+1)A; the tau's (resp. sigma's) of the rounds with C_min ≠ ∅ (resp. C_max ≠ ∅) are pairwise distinct by lem:switch in Gbar (resp. G), so B <= 2^k-1, A <= 2^m-1. Confirmed empirically on 6000 runs, both variants (1725 C_min-empty rounds, 1671 C_max-empty rounds, no violation).
- thm:readout / def:readout-cascade: every quantitative claim confirmed for n <= 7 including all 2^n Max starts and all best responses to n <= 5.
- prop:leapfrog: the parameter algebra and the K-round, K-reversal dynamics confirmed for K = 2..12; the two-player mirrored form for K <= 6.
- prop:q16: the 288-vertex game built and shown stopping, its profile values matching the normal form; both variants' runs match the printed sets; three of the four c_10 switches are val_sigma-ties.
- lem:same-successor (908 tests), prop:bsi-normal (900 run pairs on N', N_0, N_1), lem:dyadic-row (4000 rows), thm:top (200 reduced instances).

NOT CHECKED: thm:one-player, lem:normalform, lem:kblind, lem:switch, cor:comparison, lem:trapchar, prop:selfdual-bsi, prop:allswitch-overshoot, prop:no-halving beyond reading their statements to confirm the citations; the route-only 10-vertex instance of rem:readout(i) (not printed, so unverifiable); the van Dijk–Loho–Maat attribution (no web; from my own memory, unchecked against the source, their CSL 2024 "The Worst-Case Complexity of Symmetric Strategy Improvement" does prove an exponential lower bound for symmetric strategy improvement on parity games, which is consistent with the remark's flagged recollection, and the remark already flags it as unchecked).

PRIOR ART: nothing in the range is presented as new that I recognise as standard published mathematics. lem:dyadic-row's gadget is the Knuth–Yao DDG tree for a dyadic distribution (from memory, unchecked against the source: Knuth and Yao, "The complexity of nonuniform random number generation", 1976); the manuscript gives no attribution and its bound ell*d is weaker than Knuth–Yao's leaf-count optimum, which is what would give SD(K) on Theta(K) vertices. A one-line "this is the standard DDG tree" would settle it.
